articles.title: Your dandruff shampoo might help with breakouts, but there’s a catch
articles.summary: Anti-dandruff shampoos only treat one type of blemish: fungal acne. Shop the best dandruff shampoos from Head & Shoulders, Nizoral and Vanicream to treat fungal acne.
articles.body: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends (and questions) on our timelines, like whether you need pet laundry detergent to clean your dog’s things. Sometimes, the most surprisingly effective products for your skin aren’t found in the skin care aisle. Dandruff shampoos have become a viral hack for treating acne-like breakouts, with people using them as both face and body washes. But can swapping your face wash for a bottle of Head and Shoulders actually help your skin? While certain ingredients in dandruff shampoos may help with fungal acne, they won’t necessarily work for every type of blemish. I asked dermatologists to explain why dandruff shampoos may work for acne and when you’re better off sticking with traditional acne treatments. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Why are people using dandruff shampoo for acne? The idea took off on social media because there are actual results: “Many people have been fighting stubborn, itchy bumps for months with acne products that never worked, then try an inexpensive drugstore shampoo and see clearer skin within a couple of weeks,” says Dr. Mona Foad, board-certified dermatologist and founder of MONA Dermatology. “That kind of before-and-after is made for TikTok. The bottom line is that dandruff shampoo is a fantastic tool for fungal acne, but it is not an acne treatment.” Can dandruff shampoo actually treat acne? Yes, anti-dandruff shampoo can treat acne, but only one specific type of breakout: fungal acne. “Fungal acne, which we call Malassezia folliculitis, isn’t true acne at all,” says Foad. It’s caused by an overgrowth of the same yeast (Malassezia yeast) responsible for dandruff, which is exactly why dandruff shampoo works on it. The overgrowth of yeast causes inflammation and infection around the hair follicle on your scalp, forehead, chest and back, causing small red bumps that are usually mistaken for regular acne, says Katharine Perry, board-certified nurse practitioner at MONA Dermatology. But it doesn’t treat traditional acne (called acne vulgaris), which is driven by oil, clogged pores, bacteria and inflammation. That means someone with hormonal acne, blackheads or deep, painful pimples probably won’t see the same results, says Dr. Ariel Ostad, New York City-based dermatologist and reconstructive surgeon. “Many people actually have both types of acne at the same time, which is why some see partial improvement and assume the shampoo is working,” says Foad. “The bottom line is that if you have blackheads, whiteheads or deep, painful cysts, you need a true acne treatment.” Even for fungal acne, it controls the problem rather than cures it. “Malassezia yeast lives on everyone’s skin naturally, so the goal is to keep it in balance, not eliminate it,” says Foad. If you stop treating fungal acne entirely, it usually comes back, especially in hot, humid weather. So, think of dandruff shampoo as a management tool with ongoing maintenance, rather than a one-time cure, says Foad. Best dandruff shampoos for fungal acne Best overall This shampoo, which has 1% ketoconazole, is one Foad regularly recommends to her patients dealing with fungal acne on their face or body. “The key is using it as a short-contact mask, not a regular cleanser,” she says. “Lather it onto the affected areas, leave it on for three to five minutes, then rinse thoroughly. That contact time is what allows the active ingredient to work.” For the face, Foad recommends keeping it targeted and limiting it to a few times a week to avoid dryness. Best for sensitive skin Those with sensitive skin have to be careful with which anti-dandruff shampoo they use on their skin. This Vanicream shampoo is a mild option that has 2% pyrithione zinc, which has antifungal properties and targets itchiness and inflammation. It also has panthenol and glycerin to avoid overly drying out your skin, according to the brand. It’s also free of common irritants like dyes, parabens and sulfates. Best cooling This Selsun Blue shampoo comes recommended by Foad, who says the 1% selenium sulfide in its formula slows yeast growth and skin cell turnover, which can treat fungal acne and reduce flaking and scaling on your skin. It also has menthol, which feels cooling on the skin and helps reduce mild itchiness. Best budget-friendly This is a classic for a reason: Head and Shoulders’ anti-dandruff shampoo lathers well, smells good and has zinc pyrithione, which has both antifungal and antibacterial properties, says Foad. It’s also under $10, making it one of the most affordable options on this list. The shampoo combats dryness, relieves irritation and itchiness, reduces flakes and redness, and controls oil. What ingredients in anti-dandruff shampoo can help treat fungal acne? Not every dandruff shampoo has the same active ingredients, so the results can vary from product to product. The ingredients commonly in anti-dandruff shampoos that help treat fungal acne are: Ketoconazole: This is one of the most well-known ingredients in anti-dandruff shampoo. It’s an antifungal medication that helps control the yeast associated with dandruff and certain conditions that look like acne. “Ketoconazole has some of the strongest evidence for treating fungal acne,” says Ostad. Selenium sulfide: This reduces yeast growth and is sometimes used for fungal skin conditions, like seborrheic dermatitis and scalp ringworm. However, it has a strong odor and can discolor metal jewelry, so remove rings and necklaces first, says Foad.Zinc pyrithione: Like the others, this ingredient helps reduce yeast, inflammation and excess oils. While zinc pyrithione has mild antibacterial properties, it isn’t a substitute for benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid to treat traditional acne. What about salicylic acid in dandruff shampoos? Some anti-dandruff shampoos have salicylic acid, which can help treat scalp conditions like dandruff, dermatitis, scalp acne and psoriasis, experts say. It’s also a common acne-fighting ingredient that exfoliates dead skin and helps clear clogged pores. However, that doesn’t necessarily mean a dandruff shampoo with salicylic acid should double as an acne cleanser: Shampoos are formulated for the scalp and may have fragrance, strong surfactants and conditioning agents that can irritate acne-prone skin or even clog pores, says Foad. “Some also contain 3% salicylic acid, which is higher than the 0.5% to 2% range used in over-the-counter acne products and can be too harsh for the face,” she says. Using a medicated shampoo is also not a good idea if you’re using other acne products: “That’s when we start to see dryness, stinging and a really unhappy skin barrier,” says Perry. For body acne, a salicylic acid shampoo can work in a pinch on tougher areas like the back and chest, but a product designed for your skin will always be the better option, says Foad. In other words, a salicylic acid shampoo isn’t usually interchangeable with a salicylic acid acne cleanser or body wash just because they share the same active ingredient. How can you tell fungal acne from regular acne? Fungal acne and regular breakouts look very similar, but their causes are very different. In fact, fungal acne isn’t even acne at all. “Fungal acne happens when yeast that naturally lives on the skin grows excessively and causes inflammation around hair follicles,” says Ostad. That can create small, itchy bumps that look similar to pimples, especially on the forehead, chest and back. Traditional acne, on the other hand, is driven by oil, clogged pores, bacteria and inflammation. It’s not usually itchy like fungal acne is, and they’ll sometimes appear as whiteheads and blackheads (while fungal acne does not). Can you use dandruff shampoo as a face wash? Yes, and the dermatologists I spoke to actually recommend it often. “When someone has a confirmed diagnosis of fungal acne on the face, chest or back, a medicated shampoo is one of the most effective and affordable treatments available,” says Foad. It’s not limited to fungal acne either; for example, someone with seborrheic dermatitis may experience redness, flaking and irritation around the nose, eyebrows or hairline. Because yeast can contribute to this condition, an antifungal shampoo may help reduce those symptoms, says Ostad. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Mona Foad is a board-certified dermatologist and founder of MONA Dermatology in Cincinnati, Ohio.Katharine Perry is board-certified nurse practitioner at MONA Dermatology.Dr. Ariel Ostad is a New York City-based dermatologist and reconstructive surgeon. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a commerce editor at NBC Selected who has covered beauty and wellness for more than six years. I’ve spoken to hundreds of dermatologists and skin care experts to determine the best ways to treat skin and hair conditions like acne, dermatitis, dandruff and more. For this story, I spoke to three experts about whether dandruff shampoos treat acne and how to use them. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
articles.summary: Hundreds of slaves were killed by colonial leaders in the Demerera rebellion of 1823, with many survivors executed.
articles.body:
The King has made a poignant visit to the site where a Guyanese slave rebellion was violently resisted by British authorities, making the stop during his tour of the Caribbean.

He visited Independence Park in Georgetown to remember the Demerera Slave Rebellion of 1823, which saw an uprising by thousands of enslaved people.

Accompanied by Guyana's Culture Minister, Steven Jacobs, he was told how hundreds of slaves were killed by colonial leaders during the rebellion and many of those who survived were executed close to where the King stood.

Above the King was a sign that he took time to read.

"This ground was used as a public execution site," it said, "where enslaved persons...were condemned to death and hung."

The moment of reflection was what Buckingham Palace had described as the King "not shying away from the UK's colonial legacy" and described today as a chance for the King to reflect on Guyana's history of slavery and resistance.

In 2022, Charles described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to "deepen my own understanding of slavery's enduring impact", in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda .

Independence Park, which is now a sports ground, drew a crowd of dozens of schoolchildren. The King stopped to talk to many of them asking them about their homework, their holidays and if they'd had a day off school.

Outside one of the King's engagements later in the day, a small but noisy group of protesters gathered.

Many held placards saying "no apology will return what was stolen, reparations now" and "justice must not depend on wealth status and connections".

"This great wealth was built on the backs of slavery," said protester, Guyanese politician, Terrence Campbell.

"I do not want the British public to think that by me saying reparations can take various forms, it means that they do not have responsibility for reparations. They do, because the United Kingdom benefited tremendously from slavery."

The King will not be apologising for the UK involvement in the slave trade during the visit, nor will he offer reparations - compensation from those countries who benefited from the slave trade - in line with the position of the UK government.

This tour has seen a number of demonstrations so far but none have seriously disrupted the King's programme.

Royal tours often include cultural exchanges and the King's trip to Guyana saw an unusual mix up of musical styles.

On the bandstand of Promenade Gardens in Georgetown, the bagpipes of the National Piping Centre could be heard alongside traditional Guyanese drummers in a collaboration of musical styles.

Seven pipers from the National Piping Centre have been touring Guyana over the past week to learn more about the Guyanese musical traditions.

As part of his visit on Friday, the King also shared a moment with a veterans from Guyana who fought for Britain in the Second World War during an event at the Commonwealth War Graves in the capital Georgetown.

King Charles met Donald Grant, 99, who will celebrate his 100th birthday next week on November 3.

He also spoke to James Samuel, 100, who is in a wheelchair, with the the King hearing how aged 19 he enlisted in the British Guiana Volunteer Force in 1943.

"What a great pleasure it is to see you on this occasion," the King told him.

The King was waved off at the end of his state visit by Britain's High Commissioner to Guyana, Joseph Fisher, Guyana's Prime Minister Mark Phillips and a number of other dignitaries.

His departure had a small ceremonial element with the Guyana Defence Force providing a guard of honour at Cheddi Jagan International Airport.

articles.title: 30% in 2019, cancer drug margins at 700% now
articles.summary: A look at the mark-up on some of the drugs on which National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) put a trade margin cap of 30% on selling price in Feb
articles.body: A look at the mark-up on some of the drugs on which National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) put a trade margin cap of 30% on selling price in Feb 2019 shows that a majority had mark-ups of 100%-700% in the Authority's 2026 list. Citing this data, the All-India Drug Action Network, which works on access to affordable medicines, pointed out the futility of one-time MRP reduction as a policy measure in the absence of a mandate to maintain permanent margin caps along with consistent monitoring.Of the 137 anti-cancer drugs that NPPA listed for reduction of trade margin, 34 are from the 2019 NPPA list of 42 anti-cancer drugs. However, the recent list put out by NPPA, showing steep reduction in MRP, reveals that most drugs from the 2019 list that feature in the 2026 list have breached the 43% mark-up level. This level is equivalent to a 30% trade margin because while the margin is calculated as a percentage of the final MRP, the mark-up is a percentage of the price to the stockist.The mark-up in 2026 prior to the latest order was higher than it was even before the 2019 order and hence the percentage reduction in prices too is much higher in most cases now compared to seven years back. However, in the case of drugs which saw very steep reduction in MRP in 2019, the percentage reduction is lower in 2026.For example, the MRP of a brand of an anti-cancer drug Pemetrexed fell from Rs 7,000 to Rs 800 in 2019. In the latest MRP reduction, it has fallen from Rs 1,095 to Rs 297, a more modest reduction than in 2019. Many multinationals which reduced the MRP by significant amounts in 2019 have done little or no reduction this time and some originator companies - those that held the patent for the medicine originally - did not slash the MRP by much on either occasion.Only five brands from the 2019 list had a mark-up of 43% prior to the latest order, another four had mark-ups ranging from 43% to 100%. The mark-up on the remaining 39 ranged from 100% to over 700%."NPPA is calling it trade margin capping, as they did in 2019 also. That's misleading because it is not a cap. It is just a one-time reduction of MRP by restriction of the mark-up," said Malini Aisola of AIDAN adding that this would not be enough to prevent mark-ups rising again as happened after 2019.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Greenwater, California, grew into a settlement of 2,000 people following a copper discovery in 1905, but its mining boom had collapsed by 1909 without
articles.body: Greenwater, California, grew into a settlement of 2,000 people following a copper discovery in 1905, but its mining boom had collapsed by 1909 without ever making a profit. Located south of Dante’s View in the Death Valley region, the town attracted people hoping to benefit from copper mining. According to the National Park Service, water had to be hauled into the settlement and sold for $15 a barrel. As mining activity declined, residents left for other areas. Today, no ruins remain at the former townsite, marking the end of Greenwater’s short-lived mining history.What caused Greenwater, California’s copper mining boom to end by 1909Despite its growth, Greenwater faced a practical challenge in securing water for its residents and mining operations. The settlement was located in a desert region where water supplies were limited, making it necessary to transport water into the town. The cost of obtaining this essential resource was reflected in the price charged to residents and other users.The National Park Service states that “Water had to be hauled into the town and was sold for $15 a barrel.” The agency’s account identifies the expense and difficulty of supplying water as part of Greenwater’s history. Although the town attracted a population of 2,000, its development depended on mining activity that ultimately failed to generate a profit.Why did Greenwater, California’s copper mining boom collapse by 1909Greenwater’s growth did not last. The copper mining boom that had brought people to the settlement collapsed by 1909, and the mining operations had failed to produce a profit. As the industry declined, the population left the town and moved elsewhere.According to the National Park Service, “By 1909 the mining had collapsed without ever showing a profit and people left for other areas.” This account establishes the end of Greenwater’s short-lived mining boom. The settlement’s history illustrates the abrupt change from rapid population growth to abandonment after the mining activity on which it depended came to an end.What remains of Greenwater, California, after its copper mining boom endedGreenwater is now a historical reminder of the mining settlements that developed and disappeared across the Death Valley region. Unlike some former mining towns where buildings or industrial structures remain, Greenwater has no surviving ruins, according to the National Park Service. Its history is documented through the agency’s account of the early mining boom and the settlement’s subsequent collapse.The former townsite is located south of Dante’s View, off the Greenwater Valley gravel road. The National Park Service identifies the location in its historical information about Death Valley’s ghost towns. Greenwater’s brief existence, from the copper discovery in 1905 to the collapse of mining by 1909, remains part of the wider history of mining settlements in the region.You use AI every day. articles.title: 2023 Maui wildfires sparked an investor lawsuit against Hawaiian Electric, now a US judge has approved $47.75m in settlement funds while cutting attorneys’ requested fees by $4.78m after examining billing records
articles.summary: A US federal judge has approved a $47.75 million settlement in a securities lawsuit against Hawaiian Electric Industries, while significantly reducing the
articles.body: A US federal judge has approved a $47.75 million settlement in a securities lawsuit against Hawaiian Electric Industries, while significantly reducing the legal fees requested by the investors’ lawyers. The October 23 ruling by the US District Court for the Northern District of California, reported by Bloomberg Law and Law360, brings the investor class action closer to resolution nearly three years after the devastating Maui wildfires. According to the court’s order in Bhangal v. Hawaiian Electric Industries, Inc., Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley approved the settlement but awarded attorneys $9.55 million, substantially below the amount sought. The decision follows scrutiny of the legal teams’ billing records and the hours claimed for their work on the case.Why investors sued Hawaiian ElectricThe lawsuit centred on allegations that Hawaiian Electric Industries and senior company officials misled investors about the utility’s preparedness for wildfire risks. The claims concerned securities purchased or acquired between February 28, 2019, and September 4, 2023, covering the period leading up to the August 2023 wildfires that devastated Lahaina, Maui.The complaint alleged that investors were given an inaccurate impression of the company’s efforts to address wildfire threats. Hawaiian Electric and the other defendants denied wrongdoing, and the settlement does not constitute an admission of liability. The case had not reached a final ruling on the merits of the allegations. The court had previously dismissed the complaint while allowing the plaintiff to amend it. The parties agreed to settle while a second motion to dismiss was pending, avoiding the uncertainty, expense and potential delays of further litigation.Judge reduces attorneys’ fees by nearly $4.8 millionThe most significant development in the ruling was the reduction in attorneys’ fees. Class counsel requested 30% of the settlement fund, amounting to $14.325 million. Judge Corley instead awarded 20%, or $9.55 million, reducing the requested fees by $4.775 million.The judge found that the request exceeded the 25% benchmark generally applied in the Ninth Circuit without sufficient justification. The order also raised concerns about the way legal work had been recorded and the extent of potentially duplicated work between law firms.The court questioned the reported $4.6 million in legal fees calculated using counsel’s recorded hours. It estimated that reasonable, non-duplicative work would more likely support a figure of approximately $2.5 million. The judge also declined to grant the lead plaintiff’s request for an additional $10,000 award, finding that the application was not adequately supported. Separately, the court allowed $133,938.30 in litigation expenses for lead counsel Pomerantz LLP but rejected $43,297.37 in costs claimed by Levi & Korsinsky. Settlement administration expenses were capped at $500,000, despite the administrator reporting higher costs.More than 24,000 claims acceptedThe settlement administrator, Verita, received 67,472 claims after sending 160,167 notices to potential class members. Of those claims, 24,306 were accepted, while 43,166 were rejected. The high rejection rate initially prompted questions from the court. However, the administrator explained that many submissions failed to demonstrate an eligible loss, included securities or trading dates outside the class period, or lacked the documentation needed to verify eligibility.The court accepted that explanation, noting that none of the rejected claimants had challenged the denials within the available process. The approved claims represent approximately 60 million shares, equivalent to 75% of the damaged shares estimated by the plaintiff’s expert. Twenty investors opted out of the settlement, while one objection was filed and subsequently overruled.When will investors receive payments?The $47.75 million settlement will be distributed among eligible claimants after deductions for attorneys’ fees, litigation expenses, administration costs and applicable taxes. Payments will be calculated proportionally according to each claimant’s recognised loss under the settlement’s allocation plan, rather than divided equally.The court directed the parties to submit a proposed judgment by November 6, 2026. As of October 24, no payment date had been announced. The deadline to submit claims was June 25, 2026, meaning investors cannot file new claims under this settlement. If funds remain after the initial distribution, the administrator will attempt a second distribution.The securities lawsuit is separate from litigation seeking compensation for people who suffered personal injury or property losses in the Maui wildfires. The approved agreement addresses investor claims arising from alleged misrepresentations about wildfire risks, not the full range of losses caused by the disaster.You use AI every day. articles.title: The Smithsonian raised $2.5 billion a year ahead of the schedule to fund museums, research and education; the drive became the largest campaign in the history of a cultural organisation
articles.summary: The Smithsonian Institution has raised $2.5 billion through its Campaign for Our Shared Future, reaching its fundraising target a full year ahead of
articles.body: The Smithsonian Institution has raised $2.5 billion through its Campaign for Our Shared Future, reaching its fundraising target a full year ahead of schedule. Announced on 5 February 2026, the achievement marks the largest fundraising campaign in the history of a cultural organisation. Launched in 2018, the initiative brought together donors from across the United States and around the world to support the institution’s museums, research centres, educational programmes and cultural projects. The milestone comes in 2026, the year the United States celebrates 250 years since the Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776.The Smithsonian raised historic $2.5 billion ahead of scheduleAccording to the Smithsonian Institution’s official news release, the Campaign for Our Shared Future attracted contributions from more than 730,000 donors across all 50 US states and 132 countries. Around 65% of those who contributed were first-time donors, highlighting the campaign’s ability to reach people who had not previously supported the institution financially.The campaign began in 2018, although it was publicly launched in September 2024. Its original target was to raise $2.5 billion by 2026, coinciding with the 250th anniversary of the signing of the US Declaration of Independence. Reaching the goal a year early gave the institution an opportunity to look ahead to its next phase of development.The Smithsonian’s February 2026 announcement described the achievement as a defining moment for the institution and the country it serves. The fundraising total also established a record for cultural organisations, placing the campaign among the largest philanthropic efforts ever undertaken in the museum and cultural sector.The Smithsonian’s fundraising effort was designed to support its work across a broad network of institutions rather than focus on a single museum or project. Its museums, research facilities, educational centres and cultural programmes serve different audiences, from visitors exploring American history to scientists studying the natural world.What will the campaign support across the institutionThe Smithsonian’s campaign website identifies 4 main priorities for the money raised: advancing sustainability and discovery, illuminating the nation’s past, opening pathways to new knowledge, and powering creativity and innovation.These priorities reflect the institution’s wide-ranging responsibilities. Its work includes preserving historical objects, presenting exhibitions, conducting scientific research and making educational resources available to the public. The campaign is intended to strengthen these activities while helping the Smithsonian reach more people.The Smithsonian’s official announcement reported that the campaign had enabled 13 of its museums and centres to receive their largest gifts ever. The funds have supported exhibitions and programmes on the National Mall in Washington, DC, alongside partnerships and learning opportunities in communities across the country.Why was the fundraising target so significantAn earlier report published by Artnet News in September 2024 explained the scale of the campaign by comparing its $2.5 billion target with the Smithsonian’s annual budget, which was approximately $1.25 billion at the time. The fundraising goal was therefore equivalent to roughly two years of the institution’s annual budget.The report also noted that the Smithsonian’s previous major fundraising campaign, launched in 2014, had sought $1.5 billion. The newer initiative set a substantially higher target, reflecting the institution’s ambitions for its museums, research facilities and public programmes.The 2024 announcement placed the fundraising drive in the context of the approaching American semiquincentennial, the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.How does private support complement federal fundingThe Smithsonian operates through a combination of federal funding and private contributions. According to the institution’s announcement, this public-private model has helped it expand what it can accomplish for the public.Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III said the achievement reflected the generosity of people across the country. The balance between these funding sources is important to the Smithsonian’s operations. Federal support provides a foundation for its public responsibilities, while donations can help advance additional projects, programmes and institutional priorities.Congress established the Smithsonian Institution in 1846 following a request from British scientist James Smithson, who left his fortune to establish an institution dedicated to the increase and diffusion of knowledge.That original gift helped create an institution whose work has grown considerably over nearly two centuries. The Smithsonian now describes itself as the world’s largest museum, education and research complex, encompassing 21 museums, a zoo, research facilities, libraries, cultural centres and educational facilities.The fundraising achievement provides the Smithsonian with a significant foundation for its continuing work. Christine Udvar-Hazy, co-chair of the Campaign for Our Shared Future, said supporting the Smithsonian represented a contribution to the nation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: October is when the real holiday shopping starts, and this month we tried new barrel jeans, Jellycat plushies, hairstyling appliances, kitchen accessories and more.
articles.body: While fall technically starts at the end of September it often doesn’t actually feel like it until we’re well into October. Here at NBC Selected, the true signs of fall are easy to spot, not just by a breeze in the air or the crunch of leaves, but by how many seasonal sales take place. Earlier this month, we wrote about hundreds of deals during fall Prime Day, and even shopped a bunch of them ourselves. Over the course of several sale events — including Target Circle Deal Days and Walmart’s major fall sale — we wrote about, bought and tested products from categories like footwear, beauty, apparel, skin care, appliances and more. Below, my colleagues and I recommend the products we tested and truly believe are worth sharing. Some of the brands we loved this month include Adidas, Jellycat, Anyday and Bombas. The best products we tried in October 2026 All of the products below were either sent courtesy of the brand for testing or items that we bought ourselves. Cory Fernandez, commerce editor These shoes have been the ultimate casual sneaker for a few years now and every once in a while I’m inspired to shop for a new color. I recently bought a pair in a brown and white shade that would be perfect to pair with fall fits, including dark-wash jeans and jewel-toned sweaters. They’re comfortable and provide a small amount of arch support, though they’re definitely better suited for weekday commutes rather than long-distance walks. I love that they come with an extra pair of shoe laces and that the laces are long, which makes them easy to double knot. Plus, I enjoy the suede appearance over the leather — something about it feels more cozy and appropriate for this season. Ahead of the holidays and fall hosting season, this brand sent me its marvelous gift basket, which I think is the ultimate gift for a host or anyone you want to say thank you to. It’s filled with tons of salty and sweet snacks, including honey-roasted peanuts, olives, hummus, sesame treats, spreadable cheese and a bunch of international sweets, like mini cakes made in Spain and fruit jellies from Italy. Everything that comes in it would pair well with a rich fall-friendly red wine like a Rioja or Beaujolais, and the brand sells many wine gift baskets as well. Marilyn La Jeunesse, freelance newsletter editor It’s cardigan season, and this Merino wool number from Abercrombie is the perfect amount of plush and chic. While the exact one I received from the brand is now out of stock, this wool-blend option is a comparable alternative — the notable differences are the roll neck and tiny white buttons. Either way, the bright cherry red option is absolutely gorgeous — and an unexpected choice for fall that feels trendy. I’d recommend sizing down if you don’t want an oversized fit. I absolutely hate jean shopping. As someone with an hourglass figure, most jeans leave a massive waist gap, which happens when denim cuts don’t match a higher hip-to-waist ratio. I took a chance on a pair of Gap’s Curvy High Rise Barrel Jeans, ordering them in a 29 petite. I didn’t have high hopes, but I was genuinely shocked when the jeans fit perfectly (and looked good on my body). I love them so much, I bought them in two other colors and will be wearing them on rotation throughout the fall and winter. As my cats age, I’m trying to find them supplements that they’ll actually consume. They’re notoriously picky eaters, which makes it hard to invest in high-end oils without feeling like I’m wasting money. When Open Farm offered to send me a few samples, I knew I wanted to test out their Icelandic fish oil (which they make for both cats and dogs). I started mixing it into their wet food in the mornings and, to my surprise, they’ve actually been eating it. The oil (which doesn’t have any fishy odor) is packed with omegas, which helps joint mobility, skin and coat health and brain function. I feel better knowing that they’re getting a little extra nourishment in every meal. When Jellycat invites you to a Halloween party, you go. Dressed as a tired New Yorker (I definitely forgot a real costume), I loved the fully immersive event, complete with donut decorating, a Dylan’s Candy Bar buffet and a massive amount of — you guessed it — Jellycats. This year’s Halloween collection included adorable stuffed bats, gargoyles, peanuts dressed as black cats and so much more. At the end of the night, I was gifted a Rufferty Puppy ‘Wizard’ and an Amuseables Vampop Drink, both of which now sit on my bookshelf and are a welcome addition to my ever-expanding collection of Halloween decor. Shalwah Evans, senior editor At this point, Adidas needs to make me an ambassador because it seems they can’t make a shoe that I don’t like. NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin gifted these to me and the second I stepped out of my apartment the first time I wore them, someone said they were “cool-looking” shoes and asked me if they were comfy. And the answer is yes — they’re so comfortable, the break-in was about two hours and that’s only because the leather is a little stiff on the first wear. They’re the ideal commuter shoe for someone who lives in a city like NYC where you ride the train to work, refuse to do it in your heels, but still want to look good. These will probably become my main travel shoes since they’re soft, cozy and come off and back on easily. I got this face cream more than a year ago when it first launched, directly from founders Cynthia Bailey (yep, that Cynthia Bailey) and Dana Hill-Robinson to try it out and I instantly fell in love. It’s a very rich cream but it doesn’t leave my face oily or clog my very large pores. My skin is quite reactive so it will immediately let me know if something is bad or good for it, and this face cream got one of the best responses. It smells nice, it glides on with a smooth creaminess that feels like some luxe brands I’ve used in the past (I’m talking $250 moisturizers), and it absorbs quickly — a huge plus for someone (like me) who carves out very little time from waking up to getting out the door. I recently bought it and used it all up because my skin was very dry from an aggressive treatment I did to get rid of a breakout and this restored its balance in just one month. Mili Godio, commerce editor As a longtime Giggler, I’m a huge fan of ‘Bravolebrities’ Paige DeSorbo and Hannah Berner. So, when DeSorbo released the Hannah Collection for her loungewear line Daphne earlier this year, I knew I had to try it out for myself. This set exceeded my expectations: It’s super soft, stretchy and helps replace my usual oversized shirt and sweatpants with something I actually feel cute in. Plus, the matching set and neutral color makes me feel like I have my life together. The pants are definitely too long (I’m 5 foot 3, for reference), but since they’re for lounging, I don’t really mind. As a beauty editor, I’ve tried my fair share of body creams and lotions, so it takes a lot to impress me. This Kiehl’s body butter, which the brand sent me to try ahead of its September launch, is one of my favorites I’ve used all year. It’s super thick but melts into my skin in minutes, leaving it unbelievably soft and smooth. And I don’t need to use a lot to get the moisture I need, so the tub is going to last me months. There are three body butters in the collection: Creme de Énergique (bergamot and goji berry), Creme de Tranquilitê (black tea) and Creme de Amour (sandalwood and fig). They all smell and feel amazing, but the Creme de Amour is my favorite of the trio; the scent is unmatched, and the light pink color adds a little whimsy to my day. Ashley Morris, associate reporter, SEO Ever since I started taking the gym more seriously, I’ve started experiencing breakouts on my back, which is pretty typical when someone with oily, acne-prone skin like mine begins regularly sweating excessively. So I started using this Dermalogica spray, and the results have definitely paid off. Where I used to constantly have patches of texture, or even bigger, cystic acne bumps, my skin is now smooth, and I only get the occasional breakout or bump or two. I spray it after every shower, and sometimes right after I finish a workout, especially if I’m running errands afterwards — I also like that it helps fade the acne scars on my back a bit as well. I started using this lip oil while testing for a story, and as a (self-)certified lip gloss connoisseur, I can say with authority that this is one of the best glosses on the market. It covers all the basic must-haves: hydrating, non-sticky and long-lasting. But what really makes it so great is the color payoff. It’s pigmented enough to wear with a lip liner and a full face of makeup, yet the shade range is wide enough that you can also find the perfect nude for everyday, bare-faced looks. At this point I keep multiple in each bag, but the Coconut shade is definitely one of my favorites. Jem Alabi, editorial operations associate Save Khaki United sent me this striped tee to try, and it’s quickly become one of the most-worn tops in my closet. The boxy, relaxed silhouette is incredibly flattering without feeling tight, and the organic cotton, hemp and recycled polyester blend is laundered for an especially soft feel. I’ve washed mine about a dozen times at this point, and it still feels just as good as when I first got it. TikTok made me buy this one. After spotting someone wearing Fenty Beauty’s Gloss Bomb Stix in the shade $weet Whiskey, a rich mahogany color, I immediately added it to my cart, and it has since become my perfect fall lip color. It gives the pigment of a lipstick with the juicy shine of a gloss, but without the sticky feel. The formula also contains squalane, vitamin E and shea butter and is designed to lock in moisture for up to eight hours. There’s something about this sweater that reminds me of the sturdy, well-made knits my parents wore in the ’90s, which is exactly why I love it. It has a relaxed fit and slightly cropped silhouette, but it’s not so short that I have to worry about showing skin. The textured waffle knit makes a simple black sweater feel a little more elevated, and I’ve found it easy to dress up or down. It’s the kind of basic I know I’ll reach for all winter. The brand sent me this sweater to try. I’m admittedly a sucker for a good-smelling hair product, and the fruity-floral scent is what initially won me over with this Lador oil. It has notes of apricot, jasmine and orris, but there’s more to it than the fragrance: The lightweight formula is designed to add moisture and shine while helping tame frizz and flyaways. I like it so much that Lador’s perfumed shampoo is next on my list to try. Plus, it’s currently part of Ulta’s Early Black Friday sale for $25.20, down from $36. This dry shampoo has become such a staple in my morning routine that I keep a travel-sized bottle at my desk. Instead of the powdery formula you may associate with traditional dry shampoo, this is a lightweight, water-based spray that dries transparent without leaving behind any chalky residue or making hair stiff. I especially love using it to help tame my frizz and soothe my dry scalp, and the cooling, fresh feel is an added bonus. It’s also currently 30% off at Ulta, bringing the price down to $15.40. As a K-pop fan, I’m constantly spotting Korean clothing brands I want to try, but getting my hands on them in the U.S. isn’t always easy. That’s what led me to Musinsa, where I found this Muarmus jacket. It was a bit of a splurge, but the rich dark navy color immediately sold me. The faux leather doesn’t look cheap or tacky, the construction feels great and I love the silhouette. It’s become one of my favorite lightweight layers for transitional weather, and I regularly get compliments on both the fit and color. Zoe Malin, reporter Ever since Duer sent me these jeans to test, I’ve been ignoring all the other pairs in my closet. They’re made from some of the softest, most comfortable denim I’ve ever worn, and I’ve happily spent 12 hours wearing them — I genuinely don’t want to take them off. I also find their barrel shape flattering. It’s just relaxed enough without feeling baggy or frumpy, and just tailored enough to look chic. I have the dark-wash color, which I prefer for the colder seasons, but there’s a light wash, too. I’ve washed the jeans a few times and they haven’t lost their feel at all. I’ve had a hard time finding my 1-year-old, 8-pound dog Mabel a raincoat that fits her properly, is easy to put on and take off, and actually keeps her dry. I must have bought and returned at least five options by now — none of them have impressed me. But grandma knows best: My mom bought her Ruffwear’s Sun Shower Dog Raincoat this month and it checks all our boxes. It easily slips over her head and stays put on her body thanks to secure snap-closure straps and leg loops. The coat is a bit longer by the hips and thighs to keep her extra dry, plus it has an extended collar I can fold up to protect her neck from water. I put the raincoat over her harness since it has a leash portal on the back. And best of all, Mabel genuinely enjoys wearing it, and looks adorable in it. I can’t stand when a bra is advertised as a “minimizer,” yet it doesn’t actually do any minimizing. Thankfully, that’s not the case with this one from Soma, which the brand sent me to test. From the first time I wore it, I noticed that my chest appeared and felt smaller, more secure and smoother under clothes, especially in form-fitting tops, dresses and button-down shirts. The bra is incredibly comfortable, too. It doesn’t dig in or pinch anywhere, and it doesn’t feel restrictive, which is part due to the flexible, unlined mesh cups. I can wear it for hours and practically forget it’s there — that’s the ultimate goal. Bethany Heitman, commerce editor Growing up, my mom always got us the coolest Advent calendars and I’ve continued the tradition with my own kids. Not wanting to be left out of the fun, I also get my husband and myself one. This year, I chose this Sockerbit option as mine. I had received a PR email months ago alerting me to the fact that the Swedish candy company would be putting one out and made a mental note to order one when they were released — my Spidey senses told me this will be a hot item this year and I didn’t want to miss out. I live in the suburbs of New Jersey, where cave crickets run rampant. Never heard of them? They look like a mix between a dinosaur and a grasshopper. These huge, jumping bugs give me the serious ick and they commonly congregate in basements because they like dark, damp places. One way to mitigate their presence is with a dehumidifier. The one we have in our basement recently broke, so I was on the hunt for a new one. After reading endless reviews, I landed on this model from Zafro. It removes up to 150 pints of moisture daily across 7,500 square feet (great for our large basement) and is Energy Star certified. It’s also quiet and can be controlled via the brand’s app. Since I plugged it in, I haven’t seen a single cave cricket, which is the true win for me. I bought these boots for my husband, a man who wears his shoes until there are literal holes in the soles before even considering something new. His feet get freezing cold every winter, so the second I saw these, I knew they were perfect. The plush shearling lining is soft and fuzzy, the cushioned lug sole handles frigid walks to school with our daughter, and they keep him warm in the yard with our son, who insists on playing outside in any weather. Best of all, the silhouette is sleek enough that they never look clunky. I love a fidget toy and keep a whole bin of them at my desk for brainstorming sessions or whenever my hands need something to do. Putty is usually my go-to (shoutout to Crazy Aaron’s), but I was intrigued by this magnetic “putty” made of 150+ tiny, matte-coated stones. The little pebbles have such a fun texture when I mush them around in my palm, and they pack neatly into a magnetic tin. Monica + Andy may be best known for its baby clothes, but the brand just released a line of baby skin care. It sent me the full line to try, and the Soothing Baby Balm was by far the standout. As a mom, I can tell you a good balm is one of the best tools in your baby skin care arsenal. A good formulation soothes irritated patches, helps with dryness and so much more. My 5-year-old has sensitive skin, and when the button on her jeans irritated a spot on her torso, this fragrance-free balm made the redness disappear almost instantly. She’s a tough critic and hates anything that feels greasy or sticky. But she loved this balm and said it made her skin feel “so much better.” Caitlin Cusack, associate social media editor My old steamer recently broke while I was using it, so I decided it was time to invest in a reliable one. This steamer from Nori is by far the best one I’ve ever tried. It heats up in just a couple minutes and quickly takes all of the wrinkles out of my clothes — I’ve used this on light cotton, denim, heavy sweatshirts and even satin dresses. My favorite part is that the water tank is on the very bottom, so I’m not spilling water everywhere every time I try to refill the tank. It’s also clear, so I can easily see when I need to refill it. As a longtime fan of the similar Revlon One-Step Styling Brush, I was super excited to put the new Dyson AirSmooth Styling Brush to the test. My favorite part about the Dyson brush is the anti-snag bristles that are made completely of rubber. They don’t tug on my hair as much as other brushes I’ve tried, and they do a great job of taming frizz immediately. I’m able to blow out my hair in less than 10 minutes, which is basically half the time of other blow dryer brushes I’ve tried. While $250 is definitely a lot of money for a styling tool, it’s Dyson’s least expensive hair styling product and I think it’s worth it for anyone that styles their hair more than once a week. Pasta is one of my favorite foods — I probably cook it at least once or twice a week. Before I got this clip-on pasta strainer, I was using a large colander to strain (which definitely wasn’t the easiest thing to store in my tiny NYC kitchen). This is only about 6 inches long, so it can fit in almost any cabinet or drawer. It clips onto the side of your pot and catches the pasta as you pour out the water — so you don’t have to struggle to pour with one hand and hold your colander with the other. It easily drains the water and your pasta stays in the pot you cooked it in. Plus, the silicone material is heat-resistant and dishwasher-safe. I’ve definitely saved a ton of space and time since I got this less than $20 gadget. I use a blow dryer brush on my hair around three to four times a week, so I’m no stranger to breakage and split ends. I didn’t realize how much I needed a serum like this until Nutrafol sent me this one to try. It’s lightweight, super potent and does a wonderful job of smoothing out my hair immediately after I apply it. I like to use this right after washing my hair, then again after I style with my blow dryer. My hair always feels so much softer and easier to manage, and after using this for the last few weeks, I’ve genuinely noticed less breakage, fewer split ends and less frizz. The price point is a little steep for a hair serum, but a little definitely goes a long way, so I think that it’s worth the investment since I’ll have this bottle for a while. Brown is definitely my favorite color to wear during the fall, so I was super excited to try this rich chocolate tote from Aldo. I like to stuff my work bag with a ton of stuff, but hate when it gets too bulky to carry onto the crowded subways and on my walk to the office. This has three large pockets that can fit my water bottle, coffee mug, lunch and more, plus a separate sleeve for my 13-inch laptop. For me, the only thing that’s missing is one or two more internal pockets for smaller things like my keys and work ID. But, for less than $100, this tote is a great pick for anyone that wants a cute, sturdy work bag that won’t bust their budget. Kailey Sigoda, intern I recently bought these Franz pimple patches so I could finally stop wearing makeup directly on my breakouts. During Amazon Prime Day earlier this month, I bought the Dr. Melaxin patches, which are known for being ultra-thin and invisible under makeup. After trying both brands, I’ve found they are nearly identical and work great, but Franz does the job at half the price. They are 0.01 millimeters thick, so they easily hide underneath concealer while protecting my blemishes. So far, my breakouts have been healing one to two days faster since I’m exposing them to fewer external irritants. These makeup sponges were extremely popular in 2016, and one of the first makeup tools I owned. I’ve been using them practically everyday since to blend out concealer and set my face powder. While I try to wash them regularly, I’ve had my most recent sponge longer than I’d like to admit, so it was time for a fresh one. Kara Birnbaum, associate art director This shirt is the perfect elevated basic. The brand also says that each purchase allows them to give back to their community in Egypt. I thought about buying more but spending upwards of $200 on one pair is not in my budget. These Gap pants fit me the exact same and they even have pockets. I love the stripe down the side and the satin texture — truly the best answer to being casual but also looking cool. They’re such a great alternative for a quarter of the price. articles.title: Soaring cost of Halloween treats spooks shoppers
articles.summary: The price of candy, especially chocolate, is up, and Halloween bargain hunters are searching for deals and ways to cut costs.
articles.body:
Halloween shoppers in the US seeking sweet relief this spooky season have instead been shocked by the high price of seasonal treats, as cost of living pressures continue to bite.

Demetrio Beltres, a 33-year-old financial adviser searching for Halloween bargains for trick or treaters said he was spending more than his usual $15 (£11) to $20 this year because prices were much higher.

"I'm trying to spend at least $20 to $30 just to make sure that I get the kids something," he said, while browsing the rows of colour options at a Target in Manhattan.

A lot of people are finding they are in the same boat as Demetrio this year.

Stephen Zagor, adjunct associate professor at Columbia Business School, said people have only so much to spend, and when everyday essentials are costing more, people may feel less inclined to make this the most extravagant Halloween.

"I think the holiday's gotten scary, more from an economic [perspective], than it might be for scaring people at the door," he said.

Analysis from left-leaning non-profit Groundwork Collaborative and the Century Foundation found the cost of popular Halloween chocolates and confectionery was 15.3% higher this year than in 2025.

Separate research from personal finance firm Finance Buzz found prices for Halloween treats have soared by 71% over the past five years - a much bigger increase than the general pace of price rises over the same period.

The price of confectionery generally has been pushed up thanks to higher cocoa prices.

The cost of a tonne of cocoa skyrocketed to a high of more than $10,700 in January 2025, according to figures from the International Monetary Fund via the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis, as climate change contributed to severe weather which affected supplies.

"The cocoa that is now being consumed was bought when the prices were high," said Zagor, who specialises in food businesses.

Cost of living pressures have also increased, with inflation running at 3.7%, and fuel prices remain high. Diesel, at $6.32 a gallon, is only 20 cents below the record reached in September.

People shopping for Halloween treats in New York were noticing the price pressures.

"Everything is expensive, so it does not surprise me that Halloween candy is expensive too," said Mallory, who declined to give her last name.

The combined cost of living pressures have affected how much people are buying in the run up to the holiday, according to consumer and market research company Nielsen IQ. It found Halloween treat sales were down 11.7% by the middle of September, and by the middle of October sales were down 6.7%.

Chris Costagli, NielsenIQ's vice-president of US food thought leadership, said shoppers appeared more willing to spend as Halloween neared, but remained cautious.

"Sales have improved considerably from where we started in September, with smaller packs gaining ground while larger sizes continue to struggle," he said.

"This feels like a consumer who still wants the occasion, but is paying much closer attention to what goes into the basket."

How to make Halloween feel special without blowing the budget

Zagor, who is a fan of Halloween as well as traditional Halloween treats, said cutting back on costs, could present a good opportunity to offer trick or treaters a different kind of experience when they come to your door.

"It could be how you present the candy when kids come to your house as much as the one piece of candy that you're going to give," he said.

Options could include using a spooky fake skeleton hand to share out treats, rather than letting children reach into a bowl, or dressing up to meet trick or treaters.

Zagor said making your own treats is another option, inviting people over to make them together.

"You could certainly do something slightly magical, slightly interesting," he suggested.

"The trick literally could be as important as the treat."

articles.title: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
articles.summary: The second series of the hit series reached its climax on Friday after attracting 15 million viewers.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final

We've had four weeks of suspense, suspicion and very suspect tactics, as some of Britain's biggest stars engaged in a battle of wits to win the most popular show on TV.

The second series of BBC One's The Celebrity Traitors reached its climax on Friday, with the 21 original contestants having been reduced to seven before the final.

They were then whittled down to two winners - with the faithful duo of comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Heartstopper actor Sebastian "Bash" Croft emerging victorious.

The players successfully banished the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny - in dramatic fashion, and the winning pair shared the £83,000 prize for their charities.

More than 15 million people have been tuning in to this series.

Kenny reached the final stage, the endgame, after turning on his fellow traitor Maya at the last round table.

Kenny, Romesh and Bash were joined by singer James Blunt in the climax of the endgame, where the remaining contestants gather around a fire pit to decide whether they think there are any traitors left.

When James and Kenny were tied in a vote for who was a traitor, Bash persuaded Romesh to banish Kenny instead of James - thereby securing victory for team faithful.

"Absolutely devastated. Almost scraped it," Kenny seethed. "I was so close, I smelled the victory."

However, he can take consolation from the fact his performance on the show has established him as a mainstream star.

In a further twist, James chose another round of voting and was subsequently evicted himself, leaving Romesh and Bash as the last men standing.

"This might actually be the best day of my life," said 24-year-old Bash through tears of joy.

He, too, can expect a major career boost.

Romesh reflected: "I just really hope my mum's proud. And also my youngest son Charlie, who wanted me to come on the show - dad won. Please show me some respect."

The pair will split their winnings between two refugee charities, the Refugee Council and Choose Love.

Earlier, actor Michael Sheen was murdered in the first action of Friday's episode. "I am incredibly disappointed," he said. "Gutted that I got so close to the end. It's been absolutely unforgettable."

When it came to the endgame, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock was swiftly banished after Kenny voted to remove her.

"I was thinking me and him had a mutual understanding, and now I feel so stupid," she raged.

"But I'm walking away feeling super proud and like I've really accomplished something here."

Meanwhile, James B was left rueing one final mistake in a long but valiant catalogue of misjudgements throughout the series.

The singer, who looked aghast when he was attacked by Romesh during the endgame, was then the only one to choose to banish again when it came to the final three.

James was unaware that Romesh and Bash had both chosen to end the game - meaning he too could have been a winner if he had done the same - but became the victim of his own choice to banish.

"I've loved trying to work it out, I've loved getting it wrong so often, I've loved the tiny moments when I've got it right," he said wistfully. "I've loved the game."

Celebrities who departed earlier in the series included ex-EastEnders actor Ross Kemp, model Jerry Hall, sitcom star Miranda Hart, comedian Joe Lycett, presenter Hannah Fry and former BBC journalist Amol Rajan.

This series is also likely to be remembered for the two contestants who made the unorthodox decision to reveal themselves as traitors, before being summarily dispatched by their fellow players.

First, actor Richard E Grant was so giddy to have received the tap on the shoulder that he blurted out his supposedly secret status in episode two.

Comedian James Acaster, meanwhile, was the most reluctant traitor in the history of The Traitors, and unexpectedly gave himself up when he came under pressure at the round table in Thursday's penultimate episode.

There have been reports that filming of the scene was paused and he was checked by welfare staff after he became anxious.

Asked about the reports, a BBC spokesperson said on Friday that the safety and welfare of those taking part was the "highest priority", and "players are closely monitored and supported throughout by production which includes a dedicated and experienced welfare team".

Speculation about the round table being heavily edited was fuelled when eagle-eyed viewers noticed a shot of Romesh reacting in shock - apparently to James A's initial confession - which in fact seemed to have come from a later moment, after Romesh had voted for James by writing his name on the blackboard.

In the episode, the sequence where the celebrities all voted for James in light of his admission was shown as a relatively quick and straightforward process, raising a question about what prompted Romesh's shocked look.

Acaster did not take part in Friday's edition of spin-off show Uncloaked, which reunited some of the celebrity contestants following the final.

The comedian's bombshell the previous night did provide the programme with a twist to spark it to life after what some viewers saw as a mid-series lull.

On Thursday, the Hollywood Reporter noted that the show had achieved record-breaking ratings - before asking: "Why, then, has much of the consensus on social media been that it's all felt a bit dull?"

Some noted a shortage of true back-stabbing, double-crossing and explosive rows - the things, in other words, that viewers love the most - while the celebrities were more chummy and savvy than previous groups of castle dwellers.

And while there was no shortage of big characters, this season lacked an equivalent to Alan Carr, the hugely popular and apparently hapless comedian who lied and murdered his way to an unlikely victory as a traitor last year.

The drama ramped up in the final, though, and Friday's episode is likely to have been the most watched TV programme of the year.

articles.title: Can amend privacy act, revoke law if needed: Government
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Centre Friday said it is open to changing the rules of Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and, if necessary, the law itself to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Centre Friday said it is open to changing the rules of Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and, if necessary, the law itself to eliminate the possibility of its application becoming an impediment for journalists and media houses.Senior officials at the ministry for electronics & information technology said that sections of the law, which have been flagged as violative of the constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of speech and expression, are applicable to data fiduciaries and they are not for journalists."This law is only on data fiduciaries-those who keep and control data. Journalists and media houses do not come under this category," When told about the worry among journalists that DPDP Act does not expressly exempt media houses, he said, "The rules can always be amended to allay any concern on that count. The rules have the same power as the law. If necessary, we can go a step further to change the law itself."The DPDP Act has been been justified in citing citizen's right to privacy, the need to protect data and in placing obligations on data fiduciaries.Centre's reaction came days after the apex court agreed to examine a plea filed by Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) which represents 21 of India's leading news media organisations and challenged the validity of various provisions of the act and rules framed under it. The association alleged that the law was violative of the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression and threatened the full spectrum of journalistic activity.Officials said that the the concern about the DPDP act becoming an impediment for journalists will be addressed by carving out exemptions for them in the rules and, if necessary, in the law itself.I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnav said on Friday that Section 7 of the DPDP Act is for data fiduciaries like banks, telecom providers and insurance companies and media does not come within its ambit. "This govt is committed to uphold the constitutionally guaranteed rights to freedom and expression". articles.title: Manhunt under way after Toronto CEO and family violently attacked in home invasion
articles.summary: The real estate mogul and his two daughters were shot, while his wife was assaulted with a hammer, in an attack that has shocked the city.
articles.body:
Police are searching for suspects after a Canadian real estate executive and his two daughters were shot, while his wife was attacked with a hammer, during an early morning home invasion in a wealthy Toronto neighbourhood.

Derek Morton, chief executive of the Mac Group, confirmed the attack in a statement, saying: "No family should ever have to experience this."

Morton said his family was reeling from "the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home".

The suspects demanded valuables before assaulting the family and fleeing in a car, Toronto Police said. Authorities have not released the identities of the suspects.

The home invasion took place in the Bridle Path, one of Canada's wealthiest neighbourhoods, whose residents have included music stars Drake and Celine Dion.

The area is known for its large mansions behind high walls and iron gates, with hired security often seen patrolling the area.

Police said the incident happened around 03:44 EST (07:00 GMT) on Thursday morning, when the suspects entered the property through a rear door.

The suspects then confronted the family and fired their guns multiple times, wounding the father and his two daughters, and hitting the wife on the head with a hammer.

"Three masked individuals forcibly entered our residence, armed with handguns and a hammer," Morton confirmed in a statement on Friday.

"During the attack, three members of our family were shot and are currently recovering in hospital. All four members of our family were also attacked with a hammer, leaving everyone injured and requiring emergency medical attention."

Morton did not name the family members, but media reports indicate that his two adult daughters Cristina and Maggie were shot, and his wife Doriana Zohil-Morton was struck in the head with a hammer.

Two of the victims remain in hospital, police said.

Police did not identify the victims, but listed their ages as 75, 64, 28 and 26. Police said the three suspects are believed to be men in their 20s.

The police believe the family was targeted solely because they lived in an affluent area.

“Typically, in an affluent neighbourhood comes nice things – and there’s always people out there that want to acquire nice things,” Inspector Kristy Smith of the Toronto Police Service told reporters.

Smith added that police do not yet know whether the suspects took anything from the home and are working to recover bullet casings that could help identify them.

Police figures show that home invasions are on the rise in Toronto, and some residents say they are taking steps to upgrade home security.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow, who was recently elected to a second term, said she was "deeply troubled" by the home invasion.

"This attack has understandably shaken the neighbourhood and many residents across Toronto," Chow wrote on X. "This violence is not acceptable in our city. People must be safe in their own homes."

Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre called it a "horrific" incident in a separate post on X.

"These criminals must be apprehended and held accountable for their actions before the justice system," he said.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said that Bridle Path residents should expect to see increased police patrols over the coming days.

"We also continue to make strategic decisions and dedicate additional resources to address this concerning trend of home invasions and to keep our communities safe," he said.

articles.title: Ballet Cymru marks 40 years of dance in Newport
articles.summary: Ballet Cymru's founder reflects on the path that led to 40 years of the professional dance company.
articles.body:
Darius James remembers sitting before Gwent County Council at 10 years old and being asked the question: "Why should we give you money?"

He had earned a place at the Royal Ballet School, but his parents could not afford the school fees.

In response, he told the council he would go away and develop his skills and use them to help his community in Newport.

As James' Newport-based dance company Ballet Cymru marks its 40th anniversary, he hopes he has fulfilled that promise.

Growing up in Newport in the 1970s, James said it was "really, really unusual" for a boy to be doing ballet and that he was grateful for the support of his parents.

He said his father, a keen footballer who spent his life working at the Alcan aluminium factory in Newport, particularly embraced something that was so new to him.

"He didn't really understand at the beginning, but he loved it. And we work with a lot of young people now whose parents are not quite as understanding, even 40 years later, which is a bit depressing."

After years of training at the Royal Ballet School and dancing professionally, James returned to Newport and founded Ballet Cymru, originally called Gwent Ballet Theatre, in 1986.

He said the idea to start a ballet company in a post-industrial town was "totally crazy, but totally needed and logical".

"There is so much talent in Newport, so many brilliant, brilliant young people, and there's not the outlets you have in London or Cardiff."

After some initial backing from the Arts Council of Wales, he said Ballet Cymru went 13 years without any funding at all and 28 years without its own dedicated studio.

To help finance the company, James toured with other ballet troupes including Northern Ballet.

Amy Doughty, the company's co-artistic director and James' wife, joined Ballet Cymru as a dancer in 1996, and said they would rehearse wherever they could find space.

"We'd have to carry in all the ballet bars, all the equipment that we use, all the dance floors," she said.

However, with National Lottery funding in 2014, the company was able to renovate a warehouse into its current studio.

It sits on the same industrial estate James' father walked through to work each day.

In the early years, James also recalled he would cover the word "ballet" on the van they took to do community workshops because he feared it would put people off before trying.

Doughty believes attitudes have changed since then, adding: "I think we've worked really hard in Newport to go into schools, to do shows here, to really develop people who understand what we're about."

However, James believes some barriers to participation in dance remain.

The directors identified seven boys through the company's Duets scheme who they believed showed talent, only to face reluctance from some parents.

"The dads will come in and say my son doesn't dance, he doesn't want to do ballet," Doughty said.

But the pair said the children had "absolutely loved it".

Established in 2012, the scheme runs workshops in Welsh schools, where the company identifies children it believes have natural ability in dance but are not in any formal training.

Ballet Cymru then provides them with two years of free tuition. For Doughty, the financial aspect is particularly important.

She grew up in Australia as one of four children and said, without scholarships, she would not have enjoyed the same career in dance.

Doughty feels that not being familiar with ballet can stop people from engaging with the art form.

"The reality is, we've got to take it to them. They're not going to seek us out, why would they?"

She said one way they try to do this is by giving free show tickets to children participating in the Duets programme and their families.

For some, she said, it can be their first time seeing live ballet.

Ballet Cymru marked its anniversary with shows at the Riverfront theatre in Newport on Thursday and Friday, before a tour to Leeds and Bangor.

Doughty said her hope was that she and James had built something that would last and grow beyond them.

Looking back at the council's decision to support him, James said: "They believed in me.

"If in the last 40 years we've reached one kid and inspired them to be better than they would have been otherwise, then surely that's worth it.

"I'm sure it's more, but just one would be worth it."

articles.title: Why does the legend of Sawney Bean and Scotland's cannibal clan persist?
articles.summary: The legend of Sawney Bean and his family has chilled generations, telling of a murderous family who devoured people in South Ayrshire.
articles.body:
A clan of cannibals preying on unwary travellers brings to mind horror films like The Texas Chainsaw Massacre or The Hills Have Eyes.

However hundreds of years before Leatherface ever revved up his chainsaw, similar gruesome tales were being spoken of in Scotland.

The legend of Sawney Bean and his family has chilled generations, telling of a murderous family who attacked and then devoured people passing near a hidden cave on the South Ayrshire coast.

Whether Bean and his relatives ever actually existed is another matter, and still provokes different opinions to this day.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

"The first records of the Sawney Bean we know came in the 18th Century and originated in England," says Dr Gordon McKelvie, a lecturer in history at the University of Winchester who has written about the subject .

"I'm not saying there were never any cannibals in Scotland, but all these stories are written years after the alleged events happened and it feels almost safe, because 'oh, this all happened years in the past' not the here and now.

"The stories probably come from various local legends being repackaged and it was like fan fiction, where people added their own details as it went along."

The most common version of the legend has Bean born and growing up in East Lothian, but deciding to shun an honest living and moving to South Ayrshire with a woman.

Using a well-hidden cave on the coast, Bean and his family - which in some accounts of the tale number dozens - murdered passing travellers using the highway between Girvan and Ballentrae, before eating them. It was something described luridly in old tales.

However one day a man was able to use a pistol and sword to fend off an attack, although not before his unfortunate wife met a hideous end at the clan's hands.

The authorities were summoned, and King James himself led 400 men to hunt for the killers.

Upon being captured, the cannibals were taken to Leith and executed in a manner as horrible as they gave to their victims, by being dismembered or set on fire.

Hundreds of years on, and the location itself - dark and hidden - can still be unsettling, even to modern eyes.

Chris Campbell lives in Girvan and is interested in the area's myths and legends.

This led him to explore along the coast, eventually discovering one of the alleged locations for Bean and his clan.

"There was a part that was pitch black and there were three or four of us standing there in the cave, unable to see a thing," he says.

"It was unsettling. There are all these wee nooks and crannies, so you could imagine living there a bit of time before anyone would know."

Unlike McKelvie, Campbell believes there is enough published material surrounding Bean to suggest he existed in some form - but not in Ayrshire.

He believes the actual location would be in Galloway.

However the caves Campbell visited were used for illegal activity - though of a more prosaic kind than Bean's crimes.

"The myth is that it was on the Ayrshire coast, it was actually Galloway where Bean would be," he says.

"The Ayrshire myth played into the hands of smugglers, who would ship contraband to the coast. All the rumours about the caves would help keep other people away.

"But you can read enough descriptions of the trial, and the history of it, that I think he did exist."

Many of those descriptions came from publications like the Newgate Calendar, which carried sensationalist stories about crime that were often heavily embellished.

At the time of publication anti-Scottish sentiment was also high in England, while the name Sawney was considered a jibe at Scottish people, in the way "jock" would later become.

Some historians have previously said the entire legend was intended to degenerate Scots, suggesting they were so barbaric they would eat human flesh - including the claim that Bean killed 1,000 people.

Miles away from the alleged crimes, a version of the story remains a popular attraction at the Edinburgh Dungeon, where visitors are surrounded by alleged descendants of Bean who tell his story.

"It is such a good story so it has been a part of the Dungeon since we opened 25 years ago, " says Lyndsay Hebert, the venue's performance manager.

"We put you in the centre of the cave, with a person telling you exactly how they hunt people down, exactly how they will capture you and dissect you - it brings the guest into the nest of the cannibal."

The influence of Sawney Bean has since travelled far beyond Scotland.

Horror film director Wes Craven was allegedly inspired by the tales when he penned The Hills Have Eyes - about a cannibal family attacking people in the Nevada desert.

References to the legend have popped up in everything from manga series Attack on Titan to a story by science fiction writer Harlan Ellison and songs by various death metal and punk bands.

Closer to home it inspired Scottish slasher film Sawney: Flesh of Man - with David Hayman picking up victims in a taxi cab for a modern version of the tale - and Ayrshire band Junkman's Choir have a song about him.

Hebert believes the stories endure because it is still frightening to think of what humans are capable of.

"There is a primal fear there in the story that a human being is doing this to another person. It's not a monster or a creature but another human being."

That sentiment is something McKelvie agrees with, as well as its appeal to the darker part of human nature.

"Sex and violence always get an audience. As much as we balk at lurid tales in reality, we will still want to read them or watch them."
